t: Vici Twelve Week Recovery Course
84 shorter lessons for changing pornography use

This course is for people who want to change their pornography use. Each day gives you a clear idea and a practical step. You will prepare for difficult evenings, respond to urges, and make time for the rest of life.

Allow roughly three to five minutes to read and consider a lesson, its question if included, and the practice instructions. Do the exercise separately; its length is stated where needed. Reading pace varies. Work through one day at a time and adjust the pace when needed. Eighty-four days is the course length, not a recovery deadline.

The studies say what researchers tested and what the findings can support. The five named public stories are sourced personal accounts, not treatment evidence. Other everyday examples are illustrations. The suggested exercises have not been tested as a complete course.
Choose a clear rule

The exercises generally assume stopping intentional porn viewing. Write your own specific boundary on Day 1. Here, porn means sexually explicit media deliberately sought or used for arousal. Include sexual searches or accounts that repeatedly lead to the viewing you want to stop.

A slip is an action crossing your chosen boundary. A thought, attraction, dream, or accidental exposure is not a slip. Close or move past material that appears accidentally. Masturbation without porn is a separate choice discussed on Day 21.
Use the questions

Choose one for single select, or all that fit for multiselect. Follow any instruction to choose an option alone. Reflection questions have no correct answer. For knowledge questions, choose before reading the answer. All questions are optional; they do not grade recovery or prevent continuing. Mark choices on paper or in an editable copy.
Ask for help when needed

If control remains difficult and daily life is seriously affected, seek a qualified mental health or sexual health clinician. Moral disapproval alone does not establish a disorder. [1] Research on psychotherapy informs some ideas here but does not establish this course's effectiveness. [2] Ask for help before finishing when needed. In immediate danger, use local emergency or urgent support.
Keep one recovery plan

Keep one private note on paper or somewhere easy to reach. Day 1 records the starting point; later tasks add or change the sections below. Brief facts are enough. Write unknown where needed and share only what you choose.
Goal: the behaviour and your reason
Access: where devices go and what you remove
Early signs: what you first notice before browsing
First response: the first action and what follows
After a slip: how you stop and resume the day
Night routine: the next sleep period
Alternatives: activities that fit the need and hour
Continuing: returning after missed days or low motivation
Bad day minimum: a few actions for difficult days
Support: a first contact or service and a backup
Weekly life: activities and relationships to give time to
Review dates: when to check what happened

Before beginning, check how to reach qualified support and a backup. Both can be services if a safe, willing personal contact isn't available. If help is needed now, make the request now. Keep a paper or accessible copy of your response for times the phone is unavailable.

Close triggering content before opening a tool. Practising without an urge checks whether you know the steps and can follow them. Later use during an urge shows something different. Don't create urges, slips, or unsafe situations to test yourself. After a missed day, resume without restarting or doing extra lessons as punishment.

Week 1 Prepare the first week
Day 1 Prepare for tonight

It's late. Your phone is beside you, and you're making another promise about never watching porn again. You might mean every word. But at midnight, the useful decision is smaller: what will you do with the phone before you go to sleep?

Put it somewhere you can't reach from bed. Check the alarm first. If you need to receive urgent calls, keep those available. A shelf across the room is enough if leaving it outside the bedroom would cause problems. Put the laptop away too. Otherwise, you've moved one screen and left another waiting.

Think of the evening that usually goes wrong. You get into bed to answer a message. Then you check a feed. Twenty minutes later, you're searching for something you had decided to stop watching. By then, putting the phone down feels much harder. Charging it elsewhere changes an earlier decision, before that search begins.

This won't make every urge disappear. It gives you a few seconds in which you have to get up and choose. Use those seconds to begin something you've already decided on: wash, read a few pages, or turn out the light. Another search for recovery advice can wait until tomorrow if it keeps you awake beside the same screen.

Marcus Aurelius reminded himself to deal with the trouble in front of him instead of carrying every possible future trouble into it. [3] You can apply that idea tonight. You don't have to settle the coming year before putting the phone down.

Before you finish, write a few facts about where you're starting. When do you usually watch? How much time does it take, if you know? What does it interrupt? What tends to happen afterwards? Approximate answers are useful. Guessing precise numbers isn't. You'll return to these notes later to see what changed. Tonight, they only need to be honest.
Practice

Start one private note called My recovery plan. Write your porn boundary and what you know about your starting point: when you usually watch, roughly how often or for how long, what it interrupts, and what you do after an urge or slip. Write “unknown” where needed.

Prepare tonight: set the alarm, put the phone out of reach from bed, and put other devices away. Keep needed calls and accessibility available. If the device must stay close, close the content and choose a practical limit on browsing.
You are done when
Your starting notes are saved and tonight's device setup is ready.
Day 2 Remove easy access to porn

A bookmark saves you a few clicks. So does a familiar account, an open tab, or a folder you know by heart. Those small conveniences matter when you're tired and don't want to think. Today, remove one that repeatedly brings you back to porn.

Start with what you actually use. If it's a particular account, unfollow or block it. If it's saved material, delete it without opening each item for a last look. If the material is already gone, look at what still happens before you watch. Perhaps you keep opening the same feed in bed. Moving the charger may matter more than another hour of deleting files.

Wendy Wood and her colleagues studied students who moved to another university. Some habits changed when the surroundings changed; others carried over when familiar cues remained. The study looked at everyday activities, not porn, and students weren't randomly assigned to move. [12] It suggests a useful place to look: the things around a habit that make it easy to repeat.

For example, clearing your desk won't help much if the laptop still opens to the same account. Turning off its notifications might. A blocker can add another obstacle, but check its settings without searching for sexual material. Keep access to work, calls, and anything else you need.

Give this job an ending. Twenty minutes is enough for a first pass. You can spend a whole evening comparing blockers, organising folders, and calling it preparation. Stop when one change is in place. Then use the rest of the evening.

The change should be easy to describe: “I removed that account from my feed,” or “The charger is on the kitchen shelf.” Feeling determined is welcome, but it isn't the thing you'll check tomorrow. Check whether the account stayed out of the feed or the phone stayed out of bed. If the change didn't help, those details will tell you what to try next.

Day 3 Choose where to go instead

You decide to take a walk when you feel the urge. First, you check the weather. Then you choose a podcast, answer a message, and look for your shoes. Ten minutes later, you're still sitting with the phone. The walk was a reasonable idea. Starting it involved too many decisions.

Choose a nearby place now. That might be the corner shop, a short walk around the block, or the kitchen where someone else is sitting. Know what you'll do when you get there. “Go somewhere else” leaves another choice to make when you're already struggling.

Close the content before you move. Taking the same search into a different room changes very little. Put the phone away, unless you need it for safety or access, and begin the activity you chose. Make tea, sit with a book, or take the short walk. It can feel dull at first. The point is to stop spending the next ten minutes in the same search.

Check whether this works at the hour you need it. A café that's open in the afternoon won't help after midnight. A long walk may be impractical if you're caring for a child. In those cases, choose a room nearby. If moving is difficult, put the device farther away and bring a different activity within reach.

Try the steps today while you aren't struggling with an urge. Find your shoes, check the door, and spend a few minutes in the place you chose. Fix anything that makes starting awkward. This shows you can follow the steps; you'll learn whether they help with an urge when one happens.

Decide what you'll do when you return as well. Coming back to an open laptop can restart the search. Leave it closed and have the next activity ready, whether that's food, work, or bed. The walk doesn't have to solve the whole evening. It should help you start the part that comes after it.
Practice
Name an exact place you can go when browsing starts: the kitchen table, a shared room, or a safe walk around the block. Try it for ten to twenty minutes today, after closing any triggering content.

If movement is limited, change your seat or put the device away and bring another activity within reach. Keep a phone when needed for safety or access. Save the place and first step under First response.
You are done when
You've tried the change and saved the steps. If you can't try it today, prepare an accessible option and choose when to try it.
Day 4 Prepare for sleep

You finish a long day and want some time that's yours. One video feels like a fair reward. Then another begins. Eventually, the evening you wanted has taken the sleep you needed. Tomorrow starts with less energy, and the same bargain becomes tempting again.

Give entertainment an ending before you're exhausted. A programme has a final episode; a feed usually doesn't. Choose when you'll stop opening new things, where the phone will stay, and what you'll do afterwards. If work ends late, build around that. Copying someone else's early bedtime won't make your shift shorter.

In a controlled experiment, Hans Van Dongen and colleagues gave healthy adults restricted sleep opportunities over two weeks. Attention worsened across days in the groups allowed four or six hours in bed each night. Their ratings of sleepiness didn't fully track the decline. [13] This was a sleep study, not a study of porn. It does show why “I'm used to being tired” deserves a second look.

An early alarm isn't a repair for a very late night. Choose a wake time that leaves enough time for sleep. If work or caring duties keep making that impossible, the problem may need practical help beyond a bedtime rule.

Plan for being awake after the phone goes away. Leave a book nearby or choose something quiet you can listen to without opening a feed. You can make sleep easier to start, but you can't force yourself to fall asleep at a particular minute. Lying awake doesn't cancel the work you did to end the browsing.

For the next few nights, notice what you can check: when browsing ended, where the phone stayed, and whether your schedule allowed time for sleep. On Day 7, you'll look back at those details. If the stopping time was unrealistic, change it. If sleep remains persistently difficult, seek qualified help rather than adding stricter alarms. Tonight's job is to give sleep a fair chance.
Practice
Plan the next sleep period. Choose a realistic wake time, when browsing ends, where the device goes, and a quiet activity before bed. Allow enough sleep for your circumstances.
If you can't sleep, avoid restarting the feed in bed. Save the steps under Night routine and set a Day 7 reminder to check what happened.
You are done when
The sleep plan and device setup are ready. Falling asleep on command isn't part of the task.
Day 5 Have another activity ready
Stopping porn leaves a gap in the day. “Find a hobby” sounds sensible until it's eleven at night and you have no idea what to begin. Choose something you can start at the hour you usually watch.

Ask what you need then. After a late shift, you might need food and rest. On an empty afternoon, you might want company or something interesting to do. An activity can be enjoyable without improving you. A game with a friend, a meal, a walk, or a film can belong in your evening.

Katherine Milkman and her colleagues tested whether audiobooks could make gym visits more appealing. Participants in one group could listen to the supplied books only at the gym. That group initially attended more often, but the advantage weakened over time, especially after a holiday break. [14] The experiment concerned exercise attendance, not recovery. Its useful idea is modest: making an activity enjoyable can make it easier to begin.

You can use that idea without making every pleasure a reward. Play music you like while cooking. Pick a game you'd enjoy even if it did nothing for recovery. Food, sleep, and contact with people remain needs; don't withhold them to prove commitment.
Prepare the first step. Put the ingredients out, leave the book on the chair, or agree on a time to play. The familiar habit already has an easy beginning. Your replacement needs one too.

Try it for fifteen or twenty minutes today. Afterwards, ask what happened. Did you start? Did you enjoy it? Did it suit that particular hour? Those are different questions. Cooking might work on Sunday and feel impossible after a late shift. Keep it for Sunday and choose something simpler for work nights.

If an activity helps once, try it again. If it doesn't, change it. The gym study's fading effect is a reminder to look beyond the first burst of interest. You're choosing things you'd like to keep doing after the novelty wears off.
Practice
Choose an activity for the hour when you usually want porn. Match it to what you need: rest, interest, company, movement, or a break.

Prepare the materials and try it for fifteen to twenty minutes. Write whether it was easy to start and whether it helped you stop the usual browsing. Save it under Alternatives, with one adjustment if needed.
You are done when
You've tried the activity and recorded what happened. An unhelpful result is worth recording too.
Day 6 Make time for contact
Being alone can be pleasant. Spending every evening avoiding messages and watching porn may feel different. Look at how your time alone is going before deciding that you need more of it or less.

In experiments by Nicholas Epley and Juliana Schroeder, train and bus commuters were asked to speak with a stranger, keep to themselves, or travel as usual. Those assigned to speak reported a more positive experience on average than those assigned to stay alone. People making predictions had expected the opposite. [15] The finding doesn't promise that every conversation will go well. It suggests that an awkward prediction can sometimes be less accurate than a respectful attempt.

A small attempt is enough today. Ask someone about their week. Suggest a short call. Invite a friend to do something at a particular time. “Want to play on Thursday evening?” is easier to answer than “We should hang out sometime.”

You don't have to explain your porn use. An ordinary conversation can give an isolated evening some company. If you want support with recovery, ask separately and say what would help: listening for ten minutes, joining you for a walk, or helping you find a clinician. Let the person decide what they can offer.

Have something else to do if they're busy. Sending an invitation and staring at the phone all evening can make the attempt feel much more loaded than it needs to be. Leave room for a reply and carry on with your plans. Silence alone doesn't tell you what the other person thinks of you.

If you have no safe person to contact, check a class, club, community group, or suitable support service. Find out how to attend and what it costs. A regular meeting gives you another chance to see the same people. Friendship usually needs time and effort from both sides. Today, your part is to make one reasonable beginning.
Practice
Call someone, send a specific invitation, or spend time in a conversation or shared activity. Choose contact that's safe and appropriate.

If no personal contact is available, check how to join a regular group or access a suitable service. Save one option under Support. After an unanswered invitation, leave room for a reply and continue another activity.
You are done when
You've taken a contact step or checked a group or service you can access. You don't need a reply to finish.
Day 7 Review the first week
This week gave you several things to try. The useful question now is which of them made a difference in your actual evenings. You don't need to make the answer encouraging.

Suppose the phone stayed across the room on two nights. On the third, you brought it back because you couldn't hear the alarm. “I have no discipline” misses a detail you can fix. A louder alarm or a different shelf might help. But “moving the phone solved everything” also says more than three nights can show.

Look at what happened after each change. Did you leave the phone where you put it? Did you stop browsing when you planned? Could you start the activity you had ready? If something helped, name the part that helped. If it didn't, name what got in the way.

There's a difference between preparing something and using it during an urge. A quiet night can show that the phone's new charging place is convenient. It can't yet tell you how you'll respond on a harder night. Write what you know and leave the rest open. That will make the next decision easier.

Review the sleep plan from Day 4 too. Was the stopping time realistic? Did work run late? Did the quieter activity help you stay out of the feed? Keep what fitted your life and change one thing that didn't. Several changes at once can make it hard to tell what mattered.
If nothing helped clearly, choose one small change to try next week. If the problem still seriously affects your life, use the support contact you saved. Help doesn't have to wait until Day 84.

Then do something you enjoy. Have a meal, watch a film, play a game, or spend time with someone. A slip this week doesn't take that away. The course should help you spend more time living your life, including the parts that don't need a lesson attached to them.

You've recorded the review and taken time for enjoyment. A slip during the week doesn't cancel that time.
Week 2 Review and keep going
Day 8 Measure more than a streak
A streak tells you how many days in a row you've kept a rule. That can be encouraging. But it leaves out a lot of what happens in those days.

Imagine two people who haven't watched porn for two weeks. One spends every night in bed arguing with the urge until they're exhausted. The other puts the phone away earlier and gets back to a game, a conversation, or sleep. The counters match. Their evenings don't.

Researchers led by Benjamin Harkin reviewed 138 experiments on monitoring progress towards different goals. Monitoring helped goal achievement on average, though the studies covered many kinds of goals and weren't a test of this course. [16] The point for you is to record something that helps you make a decision, rather than record more for its own sake.

Choose one measure beyond the streak. You might note how much time watching took, whether the phone stayed out of bed, or whether you used the steps you planned when an urge appeared. Keep it brief. If the number is unknown, write “unknown.” A guess dressed up as a measurement won't help later.

After a slip, the earlier nights still happened. The charger you moved is still there. The activity you enjoyed is still available. A counter restarting doesn't erase those things. Look at what you can use again today.

Results can also be mixed. Perhaps you're watching less but staying up late on another feed. Perhaps urges remain strong, but you're ending searches sooner. Those differences matter because they point to different next steps. Sleep needs attention in the first example; remembering to act earlier may matter in the second.

Check your notes when you need to decide what to keep or change. If logging starts taking over the day or making you repeatedly check yourself, simplify it. A few useful facts are enough. The record should help you understand an evening, then let you get on with it.
Practice
Choose one measure besides a streak: time spent watching, nights with the phone out of bed, or whether you used your response to an urge.
Record what you know about the last seven days, with unknown for gaps. Then repeat one useful action today, or try a small version if you're still finding what helps.
You are done when
The measure and starting information are saved, and you've tried one action.
Day 9 Stop sooner after a slip
You've watched porn after deciding not to. The next thought may be, “The streak is gone, so I might as well carry on.” That thought can turn a short episode into a lost night.

The next hour still has something in it. You might sleep, eat, keep an appointment, or finish a task. Closing the screen now keeps more of those things possible. You can look at why you watched later, when you're less tired and the content is closed.

Think about what usually happens in the first half-hour after a slip. Do you keep searching? Start insulting yourself? Cancel plans? Stay awake reading advice? One of those actions may be adding more trouble than the first decision did. Choose where you'll stop that part next time.

For a late-night episode, the steps could be simple: close the content, leave the phone on the shelf, wash, and get ready for bed. For an afternoon, you might put the laptop away and make lunch. Write steps that fit the hour. A long walk isn't helpful as your only answer if you can't leave home at midnight.

Ending an episode doesn't mean pretending it had no consequences. If you missed work or broke an agreement, that may need attention. Deal with the immediate problem first, then choose a specific repair or ask for help. Repeating “I'm terrible” doesn't tell you how to do either.
Use a recent example if you have one. If you haven't slipped, prepare the steps for a possible future episode. There is no reason to create a mistake so you can practise recovering from it.

Keep the note short enough to read when you're upset. Put the first action at the top. The purpose is to help you stop sooner and resume the day, without needing to feel forgiven, motivated, or certain before you begin.
Practice

Add After a slip to your plan. Using a recent example if available, note what you did in the first thirty minutes. Then write the steps you want to use: close the content, put the device in a named place, and begin the next necessary activity.
Choose the activity for the likely hour, such as food, work, or bed. If you haven't slipped, prepare the steps for a possible episode without creating one.
You are done when
The plan names the first action, device location, and what you'll do next.
Day 10 Use the hours that remain

One missed session becomes a reason to stop training. A late start becomes a reason to abandon work. A slip becomes permission to keep watching. The original mistake gets bigger because the next decision treats the day as already lost.

Listen for the sentence that does this: “I'll start Monday,” “There's no point now,” or “I've ruined it.” Then look at what's actually left. At eleven at night, you can still prepare for bed. At eleven in the morning, you can still eat breakfast and begin a piece of work. The answer depends on the hour, not on making the day look perfect again.

Suppose you watched for twenty minutes after a difficult shift. If you keep searching for another hour, tomorrow starts with even less sleep. If you close it now, those twenty minutes remain a mistake, but the next hour can be used differently. That difference is worth protecting.

Today, try the steps you wrote yesterday while you aren't dealing with an urge. Close a harmless tab, put the device where you planned, and move to the room or activity you chose. Check the details. Can you hear the alarm? Is the kitchen available? Does the next activity need something you haven't prepared?

Fix one awkward step. A plan that says “go outside” needs an indoor option if going out at night is unsafe. A plan that says “call a friend” needs something to do if the friend is busy. The easier beginning is often more useful than stronger promises.

This practice shows whether you can follow the instructions in your room. When you use them during an urge, you'll learn something else: whether they help you stop and move on. Keep those two observations separate.
If today is going well, let it keep going well. You can practise the steps without ruining anything first. Returning after a mistake is a skill worth preparing, not a mistake you need to manufacture.

Practice
Try the after-slip steps once without an urge. Close a harmless tab, put the device where you planned, and move to the named room or activity.
Check whether it fits the hour when you usually watch. Fix one obstacle, such as an unavailable room or an unsafe late-night walk. Use an accessible option if moving isn't possible.
You are done when
You've tried the steps and corrected an obstacle if needed. No sexual content or induced urge is needed.
Day 11 Try one change for a week
An unusually easy evening can make you feel the problem is solved. A difficult one can make you feel nothing has changed. Neither evening tells the whole story.

Look at the last week. How much time did you spend watching? What happened when you noticed an urge? How did you respond after a slip or a missed task? Compare that with the starting notes you wrote on Day 1. Keep the comparison as specific as the notes allow.

For example, you might be noticing the urge sooner but still struggling to put the phone down. That's different from not noticing until you've been searching for half an hour. The first problem needs help with beginning the next action. The second needs a clearer warning sign, such as opening a particular account.

You might also be watching less while still losing sleep to unrelated videos. That is a mixed result, and it deserves to stay mixed in the record. Praising the reduction while ignoring the lost sleep would leave you with the wrong next task.

If the starting notes are thin, say so. “I used to watch most nights, but I didn't record the time” is enough. You can start a clearer note now. You don't need to reconstruct every old evening from memory.

Choose one change to try for seven days. Maybe the evening activity needs an easier beginning, the browsing needs an earlier ending, or the charger needs a different place. Change the detail that actually got in the way. Doing five new things at once makes the result harder to understand and gives you more to remember.

Put a Day 18 reminder in your notes or calendar. When it arrives, ask whether you tried the change and what happened. If the situation never came up, you won't have an answer yet. Wait until it does. Seven days gives you a time to check, not a reason to declare a result you haven't seen.
Practice
Compare the past seven days with Day 1: time or disruption from porn, responses to urges or slips, and one daily routine. Include unchanged or unknown where accurate.
Choose one change for the next seven days. Prepare it today and save a Day 18 review reminder. Write what you want to learn from trying it.
You are done when
The comparison is written, the change is ready, and the review reminder is saved.
Day 12 Repeat one useful action

“I keep watching longer than I intend” describes something you do. “I'm hopeless” claims to describe everything you are. The first sentence gives you a problem to work on. The second makes the next attempt seem pointless.

You might prefer a more encouraging description, such as “I'm someone who takes care of my time.” If it helps, use it. But give it an action. Put the phone away after brushing your teeth, or begin a short piece of work before opening a feed. Then you'll know what keeping the commitment looks like.

Phillippa Lally and her colleagues followed people repeating everyday behaviours over twelve weeks. The behaviours became more automatic at different speeds for different people. Their findings don't support a fixed number of days in which everybody forms a habit. [17] A missed repetition is a reason to look at what happened, not proof that you've missed a universal deadline.

Consider someone who plans to read after dinner. On three nights they do. On a fourth, dinner happens elsewhere and the book is at home. “I'm not a reader after all” explains nothing useful. Keeping the book in their bag might. Or they may choose a different cue on nights out.

Do the same with your commitment. If you forgot, choose a reminder you will see. If the action took too much effort, make the beginning smaller. If the event you linked it to didn't happen, decide how to handle that day. Those answers are easier to use than a verdict about your character.
Choose one behaviour for the next week and set a Day 19 reminder. You can keep the change from yesterday instead of adding another. Repeating one action is enough work if that action matters.

The notes can stay simple: did it happen, and what got in the way? Over time, they may give you reasons to trust the commitment. You won't need to argue yourself into believing a larger claim about who you've become.
Practice
Choose one behaviour to repeat for a week. You can keep the Day 11 change. Write the cue and action, such as putting the phone away after brushing your teeth.
Prepare what it needs and try it when the cue occurs. If it hasn't occurred, name the first expected chance. Record missed attempts honestly and set a Day 19 review.
You are done when
The behaviour, first chance, setup, and review are clear.
Day 13 Choose your own reason

Why do you want to change your porn use? Your answer might be sleep, time, a relationship agreement, faith, or difficulty stopping when you want to. Start there. You don't need to borrow somebody else's reason.

Beatrice, whose smoking story is published by the CDC, described how a letter from her son helped her decide to quit. She also used medication and support from people around her. [31] She had a personal reason to quit, alongside practical help. It doesn't show that caring about someone is enough by itself, or that smoking treatment should be copied into this course.

Give your own reason a sentence you could recognise on a tired evening. “I want to stop losing sleep” is clearer than “I need to become a better person.” “I want to keep the agreement we made” points to a commitment you can discuss and follow. The wording doesn't have to sound inspiring.

Guilt alone doesn't tell you how severe the problem is. Moral disapproval by itself does not establish compulsive sexual behaviour disorder. [1] A personal or religious choice can still matter to you without being a diagnosis. If you have persistent difficulty controlling sexual behaviour and daily life is seriously affected, seek qualified assessment.

Ask whether the reason has turned into an insult. “I regret breaking our agreement” names a decision. “I'm disgusting” attacks the whole person and leaves the agreement untouched. Bring the sentence back to what you want to do, protect, or repair.

Then give the reason some time today. If sleep matters, end browsing when you planned. If a relationship matters, give the person your attention or discuss the agreement honestly. If faith matters, make time for a practice you freely choose. The action should follow your reason, rather than serve as punishment.

You may still be unsure. Keep the rule about your behaviour clear while you think. You can choose to stop watching without inventing damage, illness, or a dramatic explanation for why the choice matters.

Choose one
A   To protect time or sleep
B   To have more control over what I do
C   To keep a relationship agreement
D   To follow a personal or religious value
E   Another reason

Write the reason in your own words and take one action that follows it. If you're unsure, keep the viewing rule clear while you think.

Write one sentence under Goal explaining why you want to change porn use. Name a real effect or a value you choose to follow, without an insult about yourself.

You are done when
Your reason is clear and you've taken a step that follows it.
Day 14 Return after a missed day
The newness wears off. The charger is in its new place, the lessons are familiar, and the first burst of motivation has passed. That is when a small routine needs to be easy enough to keep.

Choose how you'll return after a missed day. Open the next lesson when you have time, do one useful action, and continue. You don't owe the course several extra lessons because yesterday was busy. Turning a missed day into a debt can make coming back feel much harder.

Suppose you miss two days while travelling. When you get home, you could restart Day 1 and announce a stricter plan. Or you could put the phone back on its charging shelf and resume where you stopped. The second choice uses something you already prepared. You can improve it later if travel exposed a problem.

Keep a different answer ready for a slip. Use the steps in “After a slip,” then return to the next thing the day needs. Reading more isn't always the next useful action. Late at night, sleep may matter more.

Low motivation also deserves a specific answer. Which part has been helping enough to keep? Perhaps the phone stays out of bed even on days you don't feel like doing a lesson. Keep that. If an exercise repeatedly doesn't fit, change it instead of forcing another attempt for the sake of finishing.

Continuing also includes noticing when more help is needed. If the course is making you more distressed, or control and daily life are getting worse, talk to a qualified professional. Repetition isn't a reason to ignore that information.

Write the three answers briefly: what you'll do after a missed lesson, after a slip, and when you don't feel motivated. Use things you can actually begin. Then close the notes and use the day. Staying with a change usually involves many unremarkable returns, not a constant feeling of resolve.
Practice
Add three short answers under Continuing: when you'll resume after a missed day, how you'll use the after-slip steps, and which helpful behaviour you'll keep when motivation is low.

Week 3 Respond to urges
Day 15 What to do when an urge starts
An urge can feel like a decision you've already made. You notice the familiar thought, reach for the phone, and start searching. The few seconds before that reach are worth paying attention to.

Try describing what happens without finishing the story for it. “I want to open that account” tells you more than “I'm going to relapse.” The first sentence leaves room to put the phone down. The second can make watching feel inevitable.

Urges don't follow a timetable. Some ease quickly; others return or stay uncomfortable. You don't have to wait for the feeling to disappear before changing what you do. Close the content, move the device, and begin the next activity you chose. The urge may come with you for a while.

Suppose you're in bed and remember a video. The memory itself hasn't broken your rule. Searching for it would be the next action. Put the phone on the shelf and get ready for sleep. If you need another step, sit somewhere else briefly or read a few pages. Choose something you can actually do at that hour.

Look for the earliest sign you usually recognise. It might be opening a feed, switching to private browsing, or thinking “just a quick look.” You needn't catch the very first thought. Catching the sequence sooner than usual is still useful.

Write one sentence for that moment: “When I open that account, I'll close it and put the phone on the kitchen counter.” Keep the beginning specific. “Be strong” leaves you with another decision to make while you're already tempted.
If no urge happens today, prepare the steps and practise putting the device away. Don't search for material to test them. You can find out whether the steps help when an urge appears on its own.
Practice
Write your earliest recognisable sign of an urge and a first action under Early signs and First response. Then put the phone out of reach for five minutes without seeking a trigger.
At the start and end, notice the wish to check it. You can rate it from zero to ten. Record whether it changed, stayed the same, or wasn't there. No thought or sensation has to appear.
You are done when
The cue and response are saved, and the short observation is recorded. Zero throughout is a valid result.
Day 16 Check what you need

What was happening before you wanted porn? Sometimes the answer is sexual desire. Sometimes you're tired, annoyed, avoiding work, or filling an empty evening. There may be several things going on, or no clear explanation.

Start with the facts. You came home late. You hadn't eaten. A task was waiting. You opened the phone while sitting on the bed. Those details give you more to work with than a theory about what every urge must mean.

The next action should fit what you can identify. Hunger calls for food. A difficult email may need a first sentence or a request for help. Wanting company may call for an invitation, with something else to do while you wait. None of those steps guarantees the urge will disappear. They deal with a problem that was there before it.

Imagine someone coming home after an argument. Watching might postpone the conversation for an hour, but the disagreement will still need attention. Tonight they could stop browsing, eat, and decide when to speak again. Trying to solve the whole relationship while upset is a much larger task.

You also don't need a hidden emotional explanation for every sexual feeling. If desire is the main thing you notice, keep the porn rule clear and decide separately how you want to handle masturbation or intimacy. Another person's interest and consent matter; sex isn't a task somebody else owes you.
Today, name one likely need and one action that fits it. If you're unsure, write “unsure” and use the simple steps you've already prepared. Analysis can wait until you've closed the content.
Later, check what happened. Perhaps lunch helped with hunger but didn't change the urge. That's useful information. You met one need and still had to choose what to do with the feeling.

Day 17 Close the screen and move
You don't always have to settle the argument in your head before standing up. Closing the laptop and moving to the kitchen can happen while part of you still wants to keep watching.

Movement helps here because it interrupts what you're doing. The new room gives you a chance to start something else. It isn't a guaranteed way to remove an urge, and it doesn't need to be strenuous. Standing, wheeling to another space, or putting the device out of reach may be enough to change the next action.

Think about where urges usually happen. If it's the sofa after work, rehearse from the sofa. Put the phone down, get up, and go where you planned. Find the awkward detail now. Are your shoes elsewhere? Is the kitchen occupied? Does the next activity require a device you've just put away?

Fix the beginning rather than making the promise bigger. Keep a book beside the chair. Prepare a drink. Choose an indoor activity when going out isn't possible. If leaving the room would be unsafe or inaccessible, close the content and change the position of the device instead.

When an urge arrives, use the first step before negotiating how long you might watch. You can still feel tempted while making tea or opening your coursework. Give the next activity a few minutes before deciding whether to change it.

Today, try the steps once without an urge. That checks whether the instructions fit your home and circumstances. It doesn't establish that they'll work every time you're tempted. After actual use, record whether you stopped watching and what helped or got in the way.
If moving rooms repeatedly leaves you opening the same material elsewhere, change what happens after the move. The room was only the beginning. You still need something to do there.

Start where you usually browse. Close a harmless tab, put the device away, and move to the place or activity in your First response. Fix anything that makes beginning awkward.
At the next naturally occurring urge, try the steps and record what happened. If none occurs today, leave them ready.

You've practised the movement and saved any adjustment. The result during an urge can be recorded later.
Day 18 Prepare another activity
Changing what you do works best when you've prepared the first minute. “Find something else” is hard to follow when the phone is already in your hand.

Look back at the change you chose on Day 11. Did you try it? Did the situation happen? What made it easier or harder? If the week never included the evening you planned for, keep the reminder for the next time. There isn't a result to report yet.

Suppose you planned to cook after work instead of browsing in bed. On Tuesday you had ingredients and began. On Thursday you were hungry, the fridge was empty, and you reached for the phone. The useful change may be keeping an easy meal available. Cooking wasn't necessarily the wrong choice; its beginning wasn't ready.

Other addictions offer practical examples of preparation. GamCare's gambling guidance includes tools such as self-exclusion and planning for difficult situations. [36] These approaches address access and decisions in advance. They don't show that gambling and porn use have the same causes or need the same treatment.

For your next difficult hour, choose an activity that fits the need you noticed. Prepare what it takes to begin. If it's company, make an invitation and have another activity ready while you wait. If it's rest, avoid replacing browsing with a demanding workout. If it's a delayed task, choose the first manageable part.

You can keep the change from Day 11 when it's helping. You don't need a new technique because the calendar has reached a new lesson. If it failed, change one detail and check it after you've had a chance to use it.

An alternative may feel less immediately appealing than porn. It can still be worth doing. Judge whether it helped you stop and use the time as you intended, rather than whether it produced the same feeling.

Day 19 Check hunger anger loneliness and tiredness
HALT is a reminder to check whether you're hungry, angry, lonely, or tired. It's a short checklist, not an explanation for every urge.

The check should lead somewhere simple. If you haven't eaten, get food. If you're tired, prepare for the next sleep period. If you're angry, step away from the argument before deciding what to say. If you're lonely, consider a safe contact or a shared activity. Several answers can fit at once.

There will also be times when none fits. You may be rested, fed, and still want porn. Use the steps you've prepared instead of forcing the feeling into one of four boxes. Sexual desire doesn't need to be renamed hunger or loneliness before you can choose what to do.

Review the behaviour you chose on Day 12. Did you repeat it when the cue happened? If you forgot, place a reminder where you'll see it. If it was too much for the evening, shorten the beginning. If the cue didn't occur, wait for a real chance before judging the habit.

Consider a late shift. You might have planned to go running after work, then arrive home hungry and exhausted. Eating and going to bed could be the better decision that night. Keeping the larger goal doesn't require treating every tired evening as a test of character.

For today's practice, choose the next action from the facts in front of you. Make it small enough to begin now. Close the triggering material first; checking how you feel while continuing to browse leaves the main action unchanged.

Afterwards, note whether the basic need was met and whether you kept the porn boundary. Those are separate questions. A meal can help with hunger even if the urge remains. You can continue choosing your actions while it does.

Day 20 Notice an urge without acting on it

Urge surfing means noticing an urge without immediately acting on it. The name can sound more complicated than the exercise. You're making room for a feeling while keeping your hands off the search button.

In a study of 123 student smokers, Sarah Bowen and Alan Marlatt tested brief mindfulness instructions. Reported urges didn't clearly fall more in the mindfulness group, but that group reported fewer cigarettes over the following week. [18] It was a short smoking study, not proof about this course. It does illustrate why feeling less craving and smoking less are different outcomes.

If you'd like to try the exercise, close the content first. Sit or stand somewhere comfortable and notice what's present: a thought, restlessness, tightness, or the wish to reach for the phone. You don't have to find a bodily sensation. Breathe normally and let the feeling be there for a minute or two without searching.

Then begin the next thing you've chosen. Put the phone away, make food, return to work, or prepare for bed. The exercise needs that ending. Watching the feeling indefinitely can turn a short pause into another long evening spent thinking about porn.

If paying attention to sensations makes you more distressed or absorbed in the urge, stop. Use a different response, such as changing rooms or asking for support. This is an option, not a requirement to sit through escalating discomfort.

You can practise the steps when you aren't tempted. That teaches you how to do them, but won't tell you yet whether they help during an urge. Don't deliberately expose yourself to content to find out.

When you do use the exercise, record the next action. Did you close the content and move on? The urge may have eased, stayed, or returned. Keep that detail honest without making disappearance the condition for success.
Question

Choose one
A   Decide the exercise has definitely failed
B   Begin the next action even while the urge remains
C   Keep observing until the urge disappears
After choosing
B is the best answer. The feeling and what you do next are different things. Stop observing if it isn't helping.
Practice

Close triggering content. For two to five minutes, notice a mild urge that has appeared naturally, or practise without one. Notice thoughts or sensations if present, breathe normally, and return attention when it wanders.

Finish by beginning the next action you chose. Record the feeling and what you did separately. Use paper or memory if the phone is away. Stop and choose another response if the exercise is uncomfortable or unhelpful.
You are done when
You've tried the steps and recorded the result, or stopped and chosen another response. An urge isn't required.
Day 21 Make a separate choice about masturbation
Porn and masturbation are separate behaviours. A course about changing porn use should make that distinction clear.

For some people, masturbation without porn fits the change they want. For others, it repeatedly leads to searching or becomes difficult to stop. Some prefer abstinence for personal reasons. Choose a rule you can describe and later review, rather than assume one answer suits everyone.

Look at what actually happens. Can you keep the device away? Do you start searching afterwards? Are you choosing freely, or spending more time than you intended and missing things that matter? These questions give you something to assess without declaring ordinary desire a disease.

You might choose, for now, not to use porn and not to take the phone into a private place where you usually search. You might also decide to pause masturbation while you work out a recurring problem. State the rule plainly and set a time to reconsider it on Day 35.

Avoid turning the review into a hunt for danger in every thought. Attraction, a dream, or an unwanted memory isn't an action crossing your boundary. If an explicit image appears accidentally, close or move past it. The decision after exposure matters more than finding a label for the exposure itself.

If you have a partner, any change involving them needs discussion and consent. Sex isn't an emergency replacement for porn, and a partner isn't responsible for making your urges disappear. A rule about your own viewing can be followed even when someone else isn't available or interested.
Today, write the boundary in one or two sentences. Prepare the device or room if that makes following it easier. On Day 35, look at what happened and decide whether to keep or change the rule.
If control remains difficult and life is seriously affected, ask for qualified help. You don't need to settle every sexual decision alone before making that request.
Practice

Write your choice about masturbation separately from the porn boundary. Keep a choice that fits your values and experience. If masturbation repeatedly leads to searching, consider keeping devices away or a temporary pause.
If unsure, keep porn out of it and observe only if masturbation happens. Prepare any device change and set a Day 35 review. Add qualified support if sexual behaviour remains difficult to control.
You are done when
The choice, setup, and review date are saved. No sexual activity is required.
Week 4 Recognise and change the habit
Day 22 Understand what starts the habit

Dopamine helps with learning and motivation. It isn't simply a tank of pleasure that porn drains and abstinence refills. Neuroscientist Joshua Berke's review describes several roles for dopamine, including how it relates to reward and the effort to pursue it. [7]

The everyday lesson is easier to follow than a brain story. When a familiar activity repeatedly gives you something you want, reminders of it can prompt you to begin. The phone, the account, and the hour may become part of that habit.

Wanting also isn't the same as enjoying. You might keep searching while feeling bored or disappointed. Ask what you're doing and what it's giving you now, rather than assuming the intensity of the urge proves the activity will be satisfying.

Think about opening a feed after a long day. At first you want a break. Half an hour later, you're switching between accounts and still waiting for something good. Closing it may feel difficult even though the last few minutes haven't been pleasant. That discrepancy is useful to notice.

Today, choose one reminder you can change before the difficult hour: the phone beside the bed, a saved account, or the moment you open a feed after work. Keep the change specific. You can't make every cue disappear, but you can stop leaving the easiest one ready.
Then prepare another use for the time. A walk, meal, conversation, or hobby has its own value. It doesn't need to provide an equivalent burst of stimulation to deserve a place in your day.

Save a brief note for Day 28: what you changed, whether you used the change, and what happened. You won't need to claim that your brain has reset. What matters here is whether the evening became easier to spend as you intended.

Choose one
A   Guessing how damaged my dopamine system is
B   The account, time, or place where browsing begins
C   Ranking all enjoyable activities as good or bad dopamine
After choosing
B is the best answer. It names something you can change. The course doesn't measure dopamine or diagnose brain damage.
Practice

Choose one account, feed, time, or device location that starts the habit. Change what you can without reopening porn. If access is already reduced, check whether the setup held and fix one inconvenience.
Save the cue and first action under Early signs. Set a Day 28 check.

You've addressed a remaining cue or confirmed what works, and saved the review.
Day 23 Decide before the difficult hour

Planning ahead helps because it removes a decision you would otherwise have to make while tired or tempted. You can choose where the phone goes before you're in bed arguing about another five minutes.

One form is an if then plan: “If I open that account after dinner, I'll close it and put the phone on the shelf.” The cue is something you can recognise. The response begins with an action you can perform.

Gollwitzer and Brandstätter studied plans that specify when and where to act. In a holiday report-writing task, those who made plans were more likely to finish among participants who returned the follow-up. Some original participants didn't return it. [23] The finding supports taking planning seriously; it doesn't guarantee that a sentence will solve a difficult habit.

The plan still needs to fit the room. “I'll call a friend” leaves you waiting if they're busy. “I'll put the phone away, make tea, and send an invitation tomorrow” includes something you control now. A useful first step doesn't depend on getting an immediate reply.

Write one plan for the point where you usually start. Avoid “Whenever I feel bad, I'll do something healthy.” Neither half tells you exactly what to notice or begin. Opening an account, getting into bed, or finishing dinner is easier to recognise.
Try the steps once without an urge. Put the device away and begin the next activity. If you need materials, get them ready. If the action is too long, shorten the beginning.

When the cue next happens, follow the plan and see what gets in the way. Forgetting means you may need a visible reminder. Following it but returning to porn means the next activity or support may need attention. Those are different problems, and the notes can help you tell them apart.
Practice
Make one decision ahead of the difficult hour. Write the cue and first action: where the phone goes or what you'll begin after a named event.
Prepare the charger, materials, or short instructions. Try the beginning with harmless content. If an app or device is unavailable, prepare a paper or accessible alternative.
You are done when
The cue is clear, the materials are ready, and you've tried the beginning or prepared the needed alternative.
Day 24 Make room for food and sleep
Hunger and tiredness can make an evening harder to manage. They also deserve attention in their own right. You don't need to prove that every urge came from them before eating or going to bed.

Look at the hours you usually struggle. Have you missed a meal? Are you staying awake after you intended to sleep? Would the action you planned take more energy than you have? A demanding workout at midnight may make less sense than food, washing, and bed.

The sleep study on Day 4 found that repeated short sleep reduced attention even when people's ratings of sleepiness didn't fully reflect the decline. [13] Feeling that you can manage another hour awake isn't a reliable reason to keep postponing sleep. That finding doesn't explain every lapse in judgement, but it gives you a reason to protect a realistic sleep period.

Prepare for the actual constraints. If you work late, keep an easy meal available. If you're caring for someone, choose the rest you can get rather than a schedule you can't follow. If a phone must remain nearby for calls or accessibility, keep those functions and put unrelated browsing out of the way.

Use the Day 22 change if it's already helping. Today doesn't need another device rule. Add the missing basic care: food before the difficult hour, a stopping time for browsing, or a simpler evening activity.

Try the change once and save a note for Day 28. Record what you did, not what you assume it did to the brain. “I ate before sitting down and put the phone away at eleven” is enough to compare with another evening.

Food and sleep aren't punishments to earn through abstinence. After a slip, you still need them. Taking care of the next hour gives tomorrow a better starting point, whether today's record is encouraging or disappointing.
Practice
Look at two or three difficult moments if you have examples. Was hunger or tiredness present? If so, try one practical change: an easy meal, eating earlier, or ending browsing in time for rest.
If neither fits or you don't know, keep normal care and note what to check next time. Save a Day 28 reminder.
You are done when
You've tried a fitting change or saved an observation for later, with a review date.
Day 25 Respond to anger and loneliness

Anger and loneliness can lead you towards an activity that asks little of you and changes the feeling quickly. If porn has served that purpose, simply removing it may leave the difficult part of the evening untouched.

Name the problem as closely as you can. “I'm angry about what happened at work” differs from “Nobody cares about me.” The first suggests a situation you might address. The second may be how the evening feels, but it makes a much larger claim than the facts support.

When angry, begin by stopping the actions likely to make things worse. Close the content. Step away from the argument or message draft. Eat or rest if needed. Later, decide whether to ask a question, set a limit, or repair something you said.

When lonely, choose a kind of contact that fits. You may need more people around, a closer conversation, or support for losing someone particular. A busy feed doesn't necessarily provide any of those. An invitation or a regular group can be a beginning, though another person's reply can't be scheduled by you.

Suppose a friend cancels. You could take the cancellation as proof you're unwanted and spend the night searching. You could also make a new invitation for another day and use tonight for an activity you enjoy. The disappointment can remain without deciding the rest of the evening.
Today, choose one immediate action and, if needed, one later action on the actual problem. Put a time beside the later step so it doesn't become another vague intention.

If the feeling is persistent, overwhelming, or affecting daily life, consider appropriate support. A course exercise doesn't need to become your only answer. You can work on porn use while also getting help for a difficulty that extends beyond it.
Practice

For a known example of anger or loneliness, write what happened and one immediate response. For anger, that might be stepping away safely or delaying a message. For loneliness, try appropriate contact or check a regular shared activity.
Add a later step on the actual problem if needed. If neither feeling fits, leave the exercise aside or work with another feeling you've noticed.
You are done when
One fitting response is prepared or tried, or you've recorded that the topic doesn't apply.
Day 26 Notice when searching keeps going
“Maybe the next one will be better” can keep a search going after you meant to stop. The next clip or account promises something different, so ending feels like giving up just before finding it.

A gambling experiment by Luke Clark and colleagues helps illustrate one part of this. Near misses could increase the wish to keep playing even though they were less pleasant than wins, especially when people had chosen the play themselves. [19] It was a specific gambling task, not a study of porn. Wanting another attempt and enjoying the result were different things.

Look for that difference in your own browsing. Are you enjoying what you're watching, or mostly trying to find something more satisfying? You don't have to keep searching until the activity becomes unpleasant enough to justify stopping. The time you intended to stop is already a reason.

Choose an earlier stopping point: opening the search bar, switching accounts again, or noticing that you're bargaining for one more clip. Use the sign that you actually recognise. A rule about the tenth video is less useful if you never count them.

Prepare the next action before you need it. Close the content, leave the device where you planned, and start the activity that fits the hour. If you require the device for work, close the unnecessary tabs and open the specific task instead.

Today, practise stopping an unrelated, harmless feed when you intended to stop. You are checking a practical detail: can you notice the time and begin something else? This doesn't require seeking sexual content or reproducing the strongest urge.

Later, note what delayed you. Perhaps there was no clear ending, or the next activity wasn't ready. Change that detail. Calling the problem “novelty” may explain part of it, but the useful work is deciding where the search ends and what follows.

Choose one
A   Wanting to continue can differ from enjoying what I'm doing
B   Porn and gambling always have the same effects and treatment
C   I need to keep searching until I find something satisfying
After choosing
A is the best answer. The study tested a gambling task. Look at your own experience to decide whether repeated searching is a problem for you.
Practice
Give one harmless chapter, task, piece of music, or hobby ten minutes without unrelated feeds. Make a tally when you want to switch, then return if continuing still makes sense.
Record the tally and one observation. Add a short reminder for the next browsing urge: notice the wish for another option, close the content, and begin your first response.
You are done when
The short practice and reminder are recorded. A tally of zero is fine.
Day 27 Try movement breathing or another room
When you feel restless, tense, or worn out, choose a response for that feeling. There isn't one exercise that suits every difficult evening.

If you're hungry, food is the obvious beginning. If you've been sitting all day, a little movement may fit. If you're exhausted, preparing for sleep may help more than another task. If you're upset about something specific, you may need a pause now and a conversation later.

A shower, a short walk, stretching, or making a drink can help you interrupt browsing. Choose whichever is accessible and comfortable. These activities aren't switches that reliably reset your nervous system or remove desire. Their role is to give you a concrete action between closing the content and returning to the day.

Suppose you feel agitated after work. A long workout might be available, but it might also postpone dinner and bedtime. Try a short walk and food first if those fit better. You can decide about exercise afterwards. Making the response harder than the problem demands can keep you from beginning.

Close the triggering material before using an app or timer. If opening a tool sends you straight back into a feed, use a paper note, an ordinary clock, or no timer. The tool should help the action happen.

Try one response today. If you're not dealing with an urge, practise its steps without looking for a feeling to fix. Record whether it was easy to begin. After actual use during an urge, record whether it helped you stop and move on.

Keep one alternative for times the first response doesn't fit. Going out may be unsafe at night; showering may be unavailable. A smaller indoor action can still give you a beginning. If these steps repeatedly don't help with control, add qualified support rather than keep making the same promise stronger.
Practice
Try three minutes of gentle movement, comfortable breathing, or a change of room. Stay within your physical limits and breathe normally if a set rhythm feels uncomfortable.
Describe tension or restlessness before and after, in words or from zero to ten. Record whether you'd use the option again. Stop if it's uncomfortable.
You are done when
You've tried one option and recorded what happened. The feeling doesn't have to decrease.
Day 28 Act earlier in the habit
Habits often begin before the moment you call a choice. You finish work, sit in the same chair, open the same account, and only then notice that you're searching for porn.

Look at that beginning. Which part can you recognise soon enough to act on? Finishing dinner or opening a particular feed may be a better reminder than waiting for an intense urge. You can put the phone away at that point without first proving you're about to lose control.

Review what you changed on Days 22 and 24. Did you move the device, prepare food, or end browsing earlier? What happened on the nights you tried it? If the situation didn't happen, say so and check after it does. An unused plan hasn't failed or succeeded yet.

Keep the comparison modest. One easier night doesn't prove what caused it. One difficult night doesn't show that preparation is worthless. Look for a detail you can repeat or a practical obstacle you can remove.

For example, the phone stayed out of bed on three nights but came back on the night you needed an alarm. The next change could be an alarm solution, rather than a new argument about discipline. If the device must remain close, decide how to keep its needed functions without resuming the feed.
Write one clear cue and response in your plan. You can reuse the sentence from Day 23. Try the steps once so you're sure they fit your space, then leave them ready for the next time.

You're building a way to act earlier, not a way to guarantee you'll never feel tempted. When you notice late, the next step still counts: close the content and begin what follows. The point of knowing the habit is to make the next decision easier, wherever you catch it.
