B is the best answer. Try the scheduled sessions and review what fits; the date doesn't promise a transformation.
Practice
Choose one aim for ninety days and a realistic weekly action. Schedule four chances, then begin a small part or make the needed arrangement today.
Set reviews after two weeks and at thirty, sixty, and ninety days. Write a smaller version for difficult weeks and how you'll resume after interruption. You can reuse an existing activity.
You are done when
The aim, dates, reviews, smaller version, and first step are saved or completed.
Day 76 Give one activity your attention
Choose one input that keeps interrupting time you want for something else. It might be a feed, notifications, news, or a particular conversation.

Set it aside for twenty to thirty minutes at a time you'd normally use it. Keep essential calls, care, work, and accessibility available. Decide what receives the attention instead: a meal, a person, a hobby, or rest.

Suppose you're eating while checking several feeds. Try finishing the meal without unrelated switching. You don't have to make the room silent or pretend the feeds are harmful in every setting. You're checking whether this limit improves this part of the day.

If the input is a person, choose a respectful boundary about your own availability. Reply later when appropriate, or ask to speak at another time. Don't use the exercise to ignore urgent care or an agreement you need to keep.

At the end, ask what happened. Did you give the chosen activity more attention? Did you simply switch to another distraction? Was the limit helpful, awkward, or unnecessary? Keep the answer factual rather than claim that the mind has become permanently peaceful.
If no input is causing difficulty, deliberately choose an enjoyable activity and give it the time. You don't need to find something to remove.
Decide whether to repeat the limit. A specific rule for a meal or work block may fit better than trying to control every interruption all day. If it didn't help, adjust or leave it aside.

Peace of mind can be an appealing aim, but a course task can't guarantee it. Today's smaller question is whether one chosen part of life receives the attention you intended. That gives you something you can try again without requiring a particular mood first.
Practice

Set aside one distracting feed, notification source, or other input for twenty to thirty minutes when you'd normally use it. Keep essential functions and commitments available. Choose what gets your attention instead.
Record whether the limit helped and whether to repeat it. If no input fits, give an enjoyable activity the time without unrelated switching.
You are done when
You've tried the limit or chosen activity and recorded the result. Silence or feeling calmer isn't required.
Day 77 Schedule something you want to keep doing
Imagine a normal day a year from now. Choose one recurring activity you'd like to be part of it, rather than picture a life with no difficult moments.

You might want a class in the week, time with someone, a hobby, or a routine that protects sleep. Give the activity real dates now. You can reuse the opportunities from Day 35 or Day 75 when they fit.

Schedule four chances and make the first practical step: invitation, booking, or preparation. If the activity requires another person, give them a clear choice and prepare something you can do while waiting for an answer.

Set a review after the first session and another after four weeks. What happened? Was it worth the time? Is the schedule realistic? A future picture is useful when it helps you try something, not when it gives you another ideal to compare yourself against.

Suppose you imagine belonging to a running group. Check the actual meeting time and whether the pace and location suit you. Register or ask a question. If running doesn't fit, choose another regular shared activity. The point is the life you want to build, not a particular hobby.
We'll check the first session on Day 84 if it has occurred by then. If it hasn't, keep the reminder for afterwards. You don't need to speed up the schedule to produce a result for the final lesson.

Expect changes. Work, health, and other people's availability may alter the dates. Make a reasonable adjustment and continue rather than take the interruption as proof the year is already going wrong.
Today, leave the activity with dates, a first step, and two checks. Then let it be something you do and experience. It doesn't need to remain an image of a more impressive future self.
Practice
Name one recurring activity you'd like in life a year from now. Schedule four chances, or confirm dates already made on Day 35 or 75. Make the first invitation, booking, or preparation.
Set a review after the first session and another after four weeks. Add the first to Day 84 if it's happened by then; otherwise keep the later reminder.
You are done when
The activity has dates, a first step, and both review reminders.
Week 12 Continue after the course
Day 78 Keep the reason and next action clear
You don't have to decide how every year ahead will go before following your rule today. Keep the long-term reason clear and the next action manageable.

Read the reason you wrote on Day 13. Does it still fit? Perhaps protecting sleep remains the main aim. Perhaps your experience has made another consequence clearer. Rewrite the reason plainly if needed.

“I want to stop losing evenings to searching” is enough. You don't need a promise that urges will never return or that every future day will be easy. A personal or religious choice can also be stated without turning guilt alone into a diagnosis.

Choose one useful behaviour to keep for the next ninety days. It might be putting the phone away at bedtime, following a first response, or keeping a regular activity. Use something that has helped, rather than the strictest rule you can imagine.

Give it a review date. You can reuse a check already scheduled on Day 75. The review is a chance to see whether the behaviour remains useful and whether the support needs changing. It isn't automatic permission to abandon your porn boundary.
Use the behaviour today when its cue appears. If it doesn't, practise the first step without an urge and leave what you need ready. Don't create a risky situation to test the promise.

If the course hasn't helped enough, the long-term decision may include qualified care. Making a request for help is compatible with keeping the reason you started. You don't need to wait for one more difficult night to justify it.

Save the reason, behaviour, and date where you'll find them after the course ends. Keep the wording brief enough to read on a tired evening. A future commitment is easier to use when it tells you what to do next, rather than ask you to settle the rest of your life at once.
Practice
Keep or rewrite the reason from Day 13 under Goal. Choose one behaviour that has helped to keep for ninety days and save a review date. You can reuse a date from Day 75.
Use the behaviour today when its cue occurs. Otherwise practise the first step and keep the setup ready. Don't create a risky test.
You are done when
The reason and review are saved, and the behaviour is used or its first step practised.
Day 79 Compare the start with now
Compare the start with now. Use the Day 1 notes or earliest entry you actually have. If you're relying on memory, say so and keep the claims cautious.

Look at time spent watching, effects on daily life, what happens during an urge, and what happens after a slip. Include an activity or routine if you've been trying one. Mark unchanged, worse, or unknown when those are the accurate answers.

A mixed result can be useful. You may watch less but still lose sleep to another feed. You may stop sooner after a slip while urges remain frequent. The next action depends on the difference, so don't smooth it into a success story or dismiss it all as failure.

If the starting record is incomplete, you can't manufacture missing numbers. “I watched most evenings, but didn't record the time” is a valid starting point. Begin a clearer observation now if it will help with a decision.
Choose one decision from the comparison. Keep something that's helping, adjust a weak part, or seek more support. You don't need to change the whole plan at once.

Suppose the phone boundary has helped but the planned hobby rarely happens. Keep the boundary and ask what prevents the hobby: timing, materials, or lack of interest. Those are different from a problem with the boundary itself.

If control or daily life is worse, take that seriously. Contact a qualified professional rather than wait for the final lesson to produce a reassuring ending. The course length doesn't decide when help is appropriate.

Today, record the comparison and take a first step on the decision. Then leave the review for its next scheduled time. Looking backwards should help the next week, without taking over the hours you're trying to use differently.

D   Some things stayed the same

F   I can't make a clear comparison

After choosing
Mixed results are valid. Note what supports each answer and choose one next step. Missing entries don't prove that urges or viewing were absent.
Practice
Compare your actual starting notes with now: time or disruption from viewing, responses to urges and slips, and one routine or activity. If recalling the start, say so.
Include unchanged, worse, and unknown honestly. Choose one decision: keep a helpful change, adjust a weak one, or seek more support. Take its first step.
You are done when
The comparison and next decision are recorded, with a fitting first action.
Day 80 Prepare for a changed situation
Check whether a response you use at home can fit a changed situation. Travel, a shared room, or an unavailable phone may remove the familiar setup.

Choose one response that has helped and one likely change. Work out the first action in that setting. If the phone can't go on the usual shelf, where can it go? If going outside isn't possible, what indoor activity fits? If the app is unavailable, can you use a short paper note or remember the steps?

Try the steps once without an urge. Practise the whole response you chose, including the next activity. For urge surfing, that means the brief observation, ordinary breathing, and ending; opening and closing its page isn't the same practice.

You don't need a sensation or sexual thought to rehearse. The attempt checks whether you know what to do and whether it is practical in the changed setting. Only later use during an urge can show how it helps there.

Suppose you're sharing a room while travelling. Leaving the device elsewhere may be difficult. You could close the content, put the phone face down out of reach, and begin reading with the materials available. Keep needed calls or accessibility in mind when choosing the setup.
Save the changed first step briefly if it would be easy to forget. Don't build a detailed plan for every place you might ever visit. One likely situation is enough for today.
If no response has helped, prepare a more suitable support option instead. Check access and make an enquiry when help is needed now. Another rehearsal shouldn't delay that.
The result is practical information about where and how to begin. You don't need to claim that practice has changed your brain or made you immune to future urges to use what you've prepared.

Choose all that fit
A   Whether the steps and materials were ready there
B   What got in the way and how to change it
C   That the response will work during every future urge
D   That my brain has reset
After choosing
A and B are the best answers. Practice checks preparation. Use during an urge gives different information; neither measures a brain reset.
Practice
Choose a response that helped and a likely changed situation, such as travel, a shared room, or no phone. Prepare an accessible first step and practise the response once without an urge.
If you choose an urge exercise, practise its steps and ending. If no response has helped, check a more suitable support option and enquire if help is needed now.
You are done when
You've checked the response in a changed situation or prepared and used the needed support option.
Day 81 Use the changes that helped
Keep up to three changes that have actually helped. Choose from what you've used, not everything the course suggested.
You might keep a device rule, a first response, and a weekly activity. You might choose support and a sleep routine instead. The useful list depends on your experience.

Use the changes in today's routine. Put the phone away at the time you chose, attend the activity, or follow the response when its cue appears. If the cue doesn't happen, practise the first step and leave it ready. Don't manufacture an urge or mistake to complete the day.

Ask whether the beginning is easy to remember. A short note in the place where you need it may help more than a long folder of lessons. If a device is unavailable, keep the most necessary instructions on paper or somewhere else you can reach.
Suppose the evening rule has worked for several weeks. You don't need to replace it with something more impressive as the course ends. Keep using it and give the time to the rest of the evening.

If a change helped only because the circumstances were unusually easy, keep that uncertainty in mind. You can prepare for a likely difficult situation or seek more support without declaring the change useless.

If none has helped, don't make a list just to satisfy the exercise. Look at what's missing and take a step towards qualified help. A complete course isn't proof that the available support was sufficient.
Today's practice is use or rehearsal, not simply installing a tool or moving an object. Those preparations matter when you follow through at the relevant time.

Leave yourself a short list with reasons you recognise. It should help you remember what to do when the lessons stop arriving, rather than become another collection of rules you feel obliged to maintain.

B   A clear first response

Keep up to three actions from your answers and note when each helped. If nothing helped, take a step towards other support instead of filling the list.

Choose up to three changes that helped and use them in today's routine: device placement, a response, an activity, a sleep rule, or support.
If a cue doesn't occur, practise the first step rather than create a test. If nothing helped clearly, record what's missing and take a step towards other support.

You've used or practised the chosen changes, or taken a support step. Preparation alone isn't the whole task.
Day 82 Check how to ask for help
Other addictions can offer useful parallels about access, support, and returning after setbacks. They also have differences in risk and treatment that shouldn't be borrowed casually.

In a GamCare account, David describes returning to gambling after three years away from it. His later help included therapy, debt advice, family support, and self-exclusion. [35] It's one person's story. It shows several kinds of help addressing several kinds of difficulty, rather than one technique carrying everything.

NIDA's guidance on substance use also describes renewed use as a possible reason to resume or modify treatment. [10] This isn't proof that porn use and substance dependence are the same. Medication, withdrawal care, and other treatment decisions belong with appropriate professionals.
For your plan, check how you would ask for help. Confirm a first contact or service and a backup. Both can be services when personal contacts aren't safe or available.
Check the details: contact method, hours, cost or eligibility where relevant, and what kind of help is offered. A saved name isn't enough if you can't reach the service when you need it.

Write the opening request in your own words if it helps. “I'm having persistent difficulty controlling my porn use and it's affecting sleep and work. Can I arrange an assessment?” gives the service a clear starting point. Share only what's needed for the enquiry.

If help is needed now, send the request or make the call. Don't leave a prepared message unsent because the course hasn't ended. A reply isn't required for today's action; use the backup if the first option is unavailable.

Keep the support details alongside your first response and after-slip steps. The plan can include things you do alone and help you receive. It doesn't need to make independence the measure of success.

Choose one
A   Every problem has the same risks, medication, and withdrawal advice
B   Check the plan and seek fitting help when difficulty returns
C   A previous good period means more help can't be needed
After choosing
B is the best answer. Planning and support can offer parallels, while risks and treatment depend on the particular problem.
Practice
Confirm a first support contact or service and a backup. Check details, access conditions, and how to begin the request. Both options can be services if personal contacts aren't available.
Draft a short opening message if helpful. If support is needed now, send the enquiry or make the call. Use the backup when the first option is unavailable.
You are done when
Support details are checked and any needed first request is made. Personal disclosure or a reply isn't required.
Day 83 Finish with an honest next step
Read an early entry alongside a recent one. Choose one observation you can honestly take forward, including “no clear change” if that is what the record shows.

Perhaps you put the phone away more consistently, ended an episode sooner, or returned to an activity you value. Perhaps the same difficulty remains. The ending should fit the facts rather than manufacture a transformation because the course is nearly over.

If a remaining saved account, shortcut, or other access to porn matters, remove it without reopening the content. You don't need to inspect material first. If there's nothing relevant left to remove, don't search for something to delete.

Instead, spend fifteen to twenty minutes on an activity or person you want to keep giving time to. Use something you've already chosen. The course can end with an ordinary part of life, not another elaborate reflection about recovery.
If the record suggests a serious ongoing problem, use the support details now. The honest next step may be care beyond this course. A positive closing sentence isn't more important than that request.

You can finish with a brief note about what you'll keep and what you'll give less time to. Name real actions: putting the phone away, attending the class, keeping an appointment, or stopping repeated searches. Avoid promising that an unfinished difficulty has disappeared.
Keep the useful instructions and reminders after the rest of the material is closed. You don't need to preserve every page as something to reread whenever you feel uncertain.

Today, review the record and take one fitting action. Another deletion, a complete log, or improvement in every area isn't required. What matters is that the action follows what you've learned and leaves the next day with something clear to use.
Practice
Read an early entry beside a recent one. Note an honest observation, including no clear change where accurate.

Remove remaining access to porn only if relevant and possible without reopening it. Otherwise spend fifteen to twenty minutes on a person or activity you value. If the record shows a serious continuing problem, use the support details now.
You are done when
The record is reviewed and one fitting action is taken. A positive ending or another deletion isn't required.
Day 84 Save a short plan for after the course
Leave yourself a short plan for the next difficult evening. You should be able to find and read it without opening the whole course.

Make the first action clear. “Close the content and put the phone on the kitchen counter” is easier to follow than “remember my recovery.” Include an option for times the usual room, device, or activity isn't available.

Save a review in two weeks, and retain the thirty-, sixty-, and ninety-day checks already scheduled. At each check, ask what's helping, what's difficult, and whether more support is needed. Review sooner if control or daily life worsens.

If help is needed now, make the request now. If things are working, use the useful parts and give time to ordinary life. You don't need to keep studying the problem every evening to take the change seriously.

A missed day doesn't require restarting. After a slip, end the episode and use the steps you prepared. After a longer interruption, choose the next reasonable chance to resume. Keep the plan flexible enough for the life you're actually living.

Save the short version somewhere accessible, with a backup if the device is unavailable. Then begin the next activity you've chosen. You don't have to promise a future without urges. You have a reason, some practical steps, and a way to ask for more help when you need it.

Notes for presenting questions in the app

Place each question after the lesson and before the practice. Single select allows one answer and multiselect several. Start with no option selected. On Day 83, show only records actually entered or collected. Mark missing information and allow a cautious written comparison when no complete starting record exists.
